newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU, Boeing bound to reach accord eventually.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU, Boeing bound to reach accord eventually.

text.p: If the European Commission decides to block the merger with McDonnell Douglas, Boeing will consider "all possible options", Boeing's vice-president for European affairs Jim Frank told Reuters on Thursday.

Frank declined to list the options. But European antitrust experts thought that besides the European courts, which they said was far from a safe bet, there was little the U.S. aircraft giant could do but sit back at the EU negotiation table.

Boeing's only legal option would be to challenge the decision before the EU's Court of First Instance and, if it lost the case, file an appeal with the European Court of Justice, the bloc's higher court.

The feeling among European government officials, industry representatives and antitrust lawyers is that the proposed $14 billion merger will go ahead, the key questions being when and what conditions will finally be attached to it.
"This is a psychological war, this is playing the game of the chicken," one lawyer said.

None of the experts expected that Boeing would ignore a commission ban because this would shut it out of the EU market which accounts for 30 percent of world aircraft orders. Any EU airline ordering from Boeing could face penalities.

Few companies have challenged the European Union's merger control law to date and none has been successful. Appealing against a Commission decision takes between three to four years if both courts are involved.

The courts, in any case, would only have to judge whether the Commission respected the law, including whether it correctly assessed the product and geographical markets concerned and whether it respected the companies' right of defence.

"If it's ultimately blocked you could litigate...but you would be better advised to look again at the Commission's concerns and see whether you can structure the deal in order to win approval," one lawyer said.
The Commission is expected to prohibit the merger next Wednesday unless Boeing meets its competition concerns.
If this happened, Boeing could also ask the CFI to suspend the ban, allowing it to go ahead with the merger, while waiting for a ruling on the substance.

For this, however, Boeing, which has announced it would start trading as a merged entity next month, would have to convince the Court that far more harm would be caused by blocking the deal than by letting it go ahead.

Boeing argued in the past that the Commission should leave the U.S.'s Federal Trade Commission the lead role in reviewing the merger and follow its decision. The FTC cleared the deal unconditionnally earlier this month.

Boeing's argument is based on a 1991 EU-U.S. cooperation agreement on competition affairs which has helped the antitrust authorities solving a number of cross-border restrictive practices or clearing global accords particularly in the telecommunications market.
But the Commission has always rejected the view that the 1991 bilateral agreement applies to mergers, for which there is a clear procedure and strict deadlines.
The lawyers failed to see how the issue could be taken to the World Trade Organisation, although U.S. politicians have often threatened a trade war.
The two partners have in the past year taken several of their disputes to Geneva, including challenges of EU legislation on banana imports and the Helms-Burton Act on trade with Cuba.
"I can't see that (the merger) would qualify for the WTO," Stephen Kinsella, a partner with Herbert Smith said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton also dismissed that prospect on Thursday saying there was an "orderly process" for dealing with the merger and that he thought a trade war would "probably" be avoided.

What makes the two sides engage already in a war of words, however, is not only the size of Boeing but the strategic sector it is in. The aerospace industry is part of the national interests and even more so when it is closely associated with the defence sector, which is where McDonnell Douglas still derives its strength.
"There is very much the feeling (in the U.S.) that the Commission ought to restrain itself on a case which is of a legitimate interest for the United States," another lawyer said.

In the coming days, Boeing may -- if it decides not to make any further concessions at this stage -- withdraw the notification of the deal, which it filed for EU regulatory approval on February 18, sources close to the negotiations said.

The company would re-submit the merger agreement with appropriate modifications at a later stage, thus avoiding an EU prohibition. Provided that the changes satisfied the Commission, the deal could be cleared in a month from the date it was re-filed.
Whether Boeing will withdraw the carpet underneath the Commission's feet or whether there will a ban, the next step is likely to consist in heavy political pressure from the United States.

French President Jacques Chirac said on Thursday he fully backed the Commission in its analysis of the Boeing case, but hinted he feared other EU states could bow to the "pschycological pressure" that was mounting from the U.S.
Boeing, the world's largest aircraft manufacturer with 60 percent of the market and a monopoly in jumbo jets, has many allies in the U.S. administration and Congress.

Clinton said he was concerned by the EU's objections to the merger. Several U.S. Senators also reacted strongly accusing the Commission of defending the interests of European aerospace consortium Airbus, Boeing's only global rival.
